content.title: About
content.content: Italian, Grecian and Armenian breads are traditional bakery products, each with distinct recipes, baking methods and flavor profiles. Italian bread is often made from wheat flour with olive oil and dry yeast, giving a crisp crust and soft crumb. Grecian bread such as pita has a thin crust and a hollow interior that can be used as a pocket for fillings. Armenian lavash is thin, flexible and usually baked on an open fire, which imparts a characteristic smoky aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Italian ciabatta gets its name from the word “ciabatta”, meaning “slipper”, because of its shape.
Traditional Greek pita is baked in a “sac” oven that reaches 300 °C, creating the signature pocket.
Armenian lavash is often baked in a tandoor‑like clay oven where the dough sticks to the hot walls and quickly inflates.
In all three cultures bread is a symbol of hospitality and is usually served at the beginning of a meal.
Italy boasts over 200 regional bread varieties, each with its own ingredients and fermentation technique.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Bread provides slowly digestible energy, helping to maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in fiber (especially whole‑grain versions)
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety and nurtures a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B2 and niacin are involved in carbohydrate metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Minerals: iron, magnesium, phosphorus
items.content: These minerals are essential for blood formation, muscle function and bone health.

items.title: Low sodium content (when not added)
items.content: Homemade, unsalted bread is suitable for low‑sodium diets.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat bread contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White bread raises blood sugar quickly, which is undesirable for diabetics.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Commercial breads often contain a lot of salt; excess intake may increase blood pressure.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some industrial breads are enriched with flavor enhancers and preservatives that can cause allergic reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bread can be enjoyed on its own, used for sandwiches, served alongside soups and salads, or turned into croutons, breadcrumbs and breaded coatings. Thin Armenian lavash works well for wraps, while Italian ciabatta is often paired with olive oil and balsamic vinegar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bread in a paper bag or cloth sack at room temperature to keep the crust crisp. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag; thaw at room temperature or briefly warm in the oven before serving.
